o: Simple cricket-style simulation: numeric strings add runs, "W" increments a wicket counter, "WD" and "NB" each add one run without touching the counter, and processing halts as soon as the counter hits 10. Example 1 accumulates 1+4+6+1 = 12 with one wicket; example 3 stops after ten "W" events with score 0. Constraints are tiny (at most 1000 events), so a single left-to-right pass is all that is needed.
k: Only "W" changes the counter; "WD" and "NB" add a run but are not wickets.
The stop check must happen before processing each event so the event that makes the counter 10 is processed but later ones are not.
Digits "0"-"6" map directly to their integer values.

a.i: Walk the array, branch on the event type, and stop early when the counter reaches 10. Every rule maps to one if/else branch.
s: For each event: if counter == 10, stop.
a.t: O(L) — each event is processed at most once, L = total input length

a.i: Encode the effect of each event in a lookup structure so the loop body has a single generic update step. This scales better if more event types are added later and avoids a long if-chain.
s: Map each event to (runDelta, isWicket): digits map to their value, "WD"/"NB" to 1, "W" to 0 plus wicket flag.
Apply the mapped deltas and return the results.
a.t: O(L) — same single pass with O(1) hash lookups
a.sp: O(1) — the lookup table has constant size

w: Either approach is fine in an interview; the direct simulation is simplest. Pitfalls: treating "WD"/"NB" as wickets, checking the stop condition after incrementing instead of before the next event, and forgetting that "0" is a valid event adding nothing. Follow-up: what if extras also added balls to an over counter, or the wicket limit were parameterized.
